title: Anglo-Saxon
description: Old English month names, recorded by Bede in AD 725
origin: Bede listed the English month names in The Reckoning of Time (De temporum ratione, chapter 15) in AD 725. The English months followed the moon, so these placements are approximate. In years that needed a 13th month, the English added a third Litha month in midsummer and called the year Thrilithi.
pronunciation: Old English as scholars reconstruct it from its spelling and later sound changes; no one heard it, so the vowels and the exact sound of some consonants are well argued but not certain. Þ is th: voiced (dh) between vowels, as in Līþa, and unvoiced (th) at the end of a word, as in -mōnaþ. Ǣ is a long æ, as in cat but held, and ch in Þrimilce is the usual reading of c before e. Long vowels are held longer, double consonants are said long, and the stress falls on the first syllable of each word.

leapWeek.name: Leap week
leapWeek.meaning: The Anglo-Saxons kept their year in step by adding a whole month, a third Litha. This calendar adds a week instead, at the end of the year, about one year in six.

months.name: Ēosturmōnaþ
months.meaning: Bede says this month was named after Eostre, a goddess once honoured with feasts at this time of year, and that her name passed to the Easter festival. Some scholars doubt the goddess, but the link to Easter is certain.

months.name: Þrimilce
months.meaning: Bede's Thrimilchi: the month when cows were milked three times a day.

months.name: Ǣrra Līþa
months.meaning: The first of the Litha months. Bede says Litha means gentle or navigable, because the calm summer breezes made the sea easy to sail.

months.name: Līþa
months.meaning: In years that needed a 13th month, the English added a third Litha in midsummer, so that, in Bede's words, three months together bore the name Litha. He doesn't give the middle month a name of its own, so here it is plain Litha.

months.name: Æftera Līþa
months.meaning: The Litha month after midsummer. Bede wrote Litha for both months; the before and after forms come from later Old English sources.

months.name: Weodmōnaþ
months.meaning: Bede's Weodmonath, the month of tares or weeds, when wild plants grow thickest.

months.name: Hāligmōnaþ
months.meaning: Bede's Halegmonath, the month of sacred rites, probably offerings for the harvest.

months.name: Winterfylleþ
months.meaning: Bede says the English counted winter as starting at this month's full moon, which gave it its name.

months.name: Blōtmōnaþ
months.meaning: Bede's Blodmonath, the month of offerings, when cattle that couldn't be kept through winter were slaughtered and dedicated to the gods.

months.name: Ǣrra Gēola
months.meaning: The month before Yule, the midwinter feast. Bede says the name Giuli comes from the turning of the sun, when the days begin to lengthen again.

months.name: Æftera Gēola
months.meaning: The month after Yule. Bede used the one name, Giuli, for both December and January.

months.name: Solmōnaþ
months.meaning: Bede says this was the month of cakes, which the English offered to their gods.

months.name: Hrēþmōnaþ
months.meaning: Bede says it was named after Hretha, a goddess who received offerings in this month. Nothing else is known about her.

festivals.name: Mōdraniht
festivals.meaning: Bede, writing in 725, says the English year began on 25 December and that the night before was called Modranecht, 'mothers' night', probably because of rites held then. He does not describe the rites. Here it falls on 24 December.

festivals.name: Gēola
festivals.meaning: Bede names the months around midwinter Giuli, and Yule is the feast the name points to, though he does not describe it. Here it is dated to the December solstice, a modern choice, since Bede ties the year's start to 25 December.

festivals.name: Līþa
festivals.meaning: Bede gives Litha as the name of both the June and July months, which he glosses as 'gentle' or 'navigable' for the calm winds and seas. He describes no festival. Here the season is marked at the June solstice by modern convention.
